lesson.title: Activation Energy: The Hill Every Reaction Must Climb
lesson.summary: Defines activation energy as the minimum collision energy needed to react, read directly off a reaction energy diagram, and shows why even energy-releasing reactions still require it.
lesson.body:
Activation energy, given the symbol Ea, is the minimum kinetic energy that colliding particles must bring to the collision, concentrated along the line connecting them at the moment of impact, for that collision to have any chance of becoming a reaction, even assuming perfect orientation. This is exactly the "sufficient energy" requirement introduced in the previous section on collision theory, now given a precise, quantitative name.

The clearest way to picture Ea is on a reaction energy diagram: potential energy on the vertical axis, progress of the reaction (the reaction coordinate) on the horizontal axis. Reactants start at some energy on the left, must climb up and over a hill, an energy barrier, before descending down to products on the right. Activation energy is the height of that hill measured starting from the reactants' own energy level, not measured from the very bottom of the whole diagram. Because kinetic molecular theory already establishes that particles exist across a distribution of kinetic energies rather than all moving at one identical speed, only the collisions between particles that happen to both be moving fast enough, specifically whose combined energy directed along the collision axis exceeds Ea, even have a chance of reacting. Raising the temperature shifts that whole distribution toward higher energies, which is why reactions with a given Ea generally speed up as temperature rises, though the precise mathematical relationship between temperature and rate is developed elsewhere in this course.

Worked example, reading Ea directly off an energy diagram. Suppose reactants sit at 40 kJ/mol, the peak of the energy barrier sits at 125 kJ/mol, and products sit at 10 kJ/mol, all measured relative to the same common reference point.

Ea (forward direction) = peak minus reactants = 125 - 40 = 85 kJ/mol
Ea (reverse direction) = peak minus products = 125 - 10 = 115 kJ/mol
Overall reaction energy change = products minus reactants = 10 - 40 = -30 kJ/mol, an exothermic reaction, since energy is released overall

Notice something worth sitting with: this reaction is exothermic, releasing 30 kJ/mol net, and yet it still has to climb an 85 kJ/mol hill to get there. Being energetically downhill overall does not mean a reaction happens instantly or without resistance; the activation energy barrier has to be overcome regardless of whether the destination is higher or lower in energy than the starting point. A higher Ea generally means a slower reaction at a given temperature, simply because fewer particles in the kinetic energy distribution have enough energy to clear a taller barrier.

That peak point on the diagram, sitting at 125 kJ/mol in the worked example above, is not just an abstract number on a graph. It corresponds to an actual, if extraordinarily short lived, arrangement of atoms partway between reactants and products. Describing that arrangement in structural terms is exactly the job of the next two sections, activated complex and transition state.
